analytic.title: Minimal Schedulability Testing Interval for Real-Time Periodic Tasks with Arbitrary Release Offsets

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The concept of feasibility (or schedulability) interval plays a very important role in the schedulability analysis in real-time systems. Existing results on the schedulability testing interval of real-time task sets under fixed priority scheduling with arbitrary release offsets (or phases) have limitations for certain scenarios in constructing a schedule for testing the schedulability of a given task set. In this paper, we propose a transforming method for deriving minimal schedulability testing interval of real-time n-task sets with arbitrary release offsets under fixed priority scheduling in both the classical preemptive model and the Priority-based Functional Reactive Programming (P-FRP) model on uniprocessor. The complexity of our transforming method is O(n), and the validity is also proved by theoretical analysis.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In our modern society, the need for real-time embedded system is becoming increasingly strong, and developments of cyber-physical systems are also attracting more and more attentions. In the design of a real-time system, schedulability analysis is a very important step for ensuring the timing requirements of the system to be fulfilled, and the feasibility (or schedulability) interval of given task sets plays a very important role in the step of schedulability analysis.

Fixed priority scheduling is one of the influential policies for scheduling real-time tasks, and the classical preemptive model [1] (shortened as the classical model in the rest of this paper) is one of the most important task schedule models and has received extensive study [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7]. For modeling and implementing safety-critical embedded systems, the Functional Reactive Programming (FRP) [8] has been proposed and gotten widely used in preemptive reactive systems. Recently, as a variant of the FRP model, the prioritybased (preemptive) functional reactive programming (P-FRP) model [9] has been proposed, which maintains both type-safety and state-less execution paradigm of FRP, and supports assigning different priorities to different tasks while not requiring the use of synchronization mechanism between tasks in real-time systems. P-FRP is at the frontier of embedded and real-time system research, and it has the potential to transform the implementation of the control components of future complex cyber-physical systems. Its potential is recognized by two US NSF research awards (*) supporting work in P-FRP and its schedulability and response time analysis. Our preliminary results demonstrate the impact of P-FRP in building safer controllers in automobile anti-lock brake systems [10].

In both the classical and P-FRP models, particular interest has been devoted in the literature to the schedulability testing interval of real-time task sets with arbitrary release offsets under fixed priority scheduling on uniprocessor. However, the main limitation of previous results is that the length of the schedulability testing interval in previous work could be rather long (see Sec. II for details) and checking the schedulability within such a long interval is time and memory consuming.

div.head: A. Contributions
div.p: In this paper, we propose a transforming method for deriving minimal schedulability testing interval of real-time ntask sets with arbitrary release offsets under fixed priority scheduling on uniprocessor in both the classical and P-FRP models. The existing limitations are eliminated and the maximum interval length for checking the schedulability is bounded. The validity of our method is proved by theoretical analysis and the complexity of the transformation is O(n).

div.head: B. Basic Concepts and Notations
div.p: In this subsection, we introduce the system model, some basic concepts and notations used in the paper.

We consider a hard real-time uniprocessor system in the classical model or P-FRP model with an n-task set * n = {τ 1 ,τ 2 ,...,τ n } of periodic tasks under fixed priority scheduling. The start-up of the system is assumed to be at the absolute time 0. All tasks are independent, i.e., requests for any τ i are not dependent on the initiation or completion of any other tasks. For later notational convenience, we label the tasks to indicate that task τ i is assigned a unique fixed priority i (1 d i d n), where 1 is the highest priority and n is the lowest. In the paper, all values of i, j, k, m, and n are natural numbers.

Each periodic task τ i is characterized by a (maximum) computation time C i , a constant arrival time period T i between two successive jobs (or instances, invocations) of the task, and a relative deadline D i , and a release offset (or phasing) ) ) i . These temporal parameters of tasks are assumed to be natural numbers. The release offset ) i is the release time, relative to time 0, of the first job of the task τ i . Without loss of generality, we assume 0<C i d min{D i , T i }, for all i, 1 d i d n.

For each k, 1 d k d n, let * * k ={τ 1 ,τ 2 ,...,τ k } * n to be the first k higher priority tasks. Let LCM k =LCM(T 1 ,T 2 ,...,T k ) to denote the least common multiple (LCM) of the first k higher priority tasks' periods, and LCM 1 =T 1 . In the literature, the hyperperiod H (or L, P) is also used for denoting the LCM of all task periods. Periodic task sets may be scheduled in a synchronous way if there is some time point at which all tasks arrive at the same time, or in an asynchronous way where all tasks never arrive simultaneously. Tasks with common release must be synchronous. However, tasks with different release offsets do not implies they are asynchronous tasks, since they may arrive at the same time some later. For example, when all task periods are co-prime, the task set must experience a common release, regardless of any imposed offsets [12], [16]. Notice that for an asynchronous scheduling there may still be some tasks (but never all) sharing a common release.

A task is referred to as schedulable according to a given scheduling policy if its worst-case response time under that scheduling policy is less than or equal to its deadline. Similarly, a task set is referred to as schedulable according to a given scheduling policy if all of its tasks are schedulable.

A feasibility interval is the time interval [t, t+H) such that if all tasks are schedulable in [t, t+H) then the tasks will also be schedulable in the time interval [0, Z): Z + [11], [12], [15]. A schedulability testing interval [a, b) is the time interval in which the schedulability of a given task set is checked. In general, the length of [a, b) is no less than that of [t, t+H).
We assume that a task can only be preempted at discrete (integer) time instants, and the cost of preemption is zero. Further, we assume that once a job starts to execute it will not suspend itself.

div.head: C. Organization
div.p: The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Sec. II gives a brief overview on related work. Sec. III presents our new results, including theoretical analysis of our transforming method, and Sec. IV concludes the paper.

div.head: III. NEW SCHEDULABILITY TESTING INTERVAL
div.p: In this section, we propose new schedulability testing interval for hard real-time n-task sets with arbitrary release offsets under fixed priority scheduling on uniprocessor system. Notice that, for any periodic n-task sets on uniprocessor, under both fixed and dynamic priority preemptive scheduling, if the length of a feasibility interval is LCM n , such as [S n , S n +LCM n ) in [13], then, it is applicable to both the classical and P-FRP models, since all periods of tasks have been taken into account, and thus, for certain given priorities and release order, within a length of LCM n , all possible release, execution, and preemption states between tasks have been covered after some stabilization time point S n . Therefore, a feasibility interval will have nothing to do with execution paradigm of a model. However, if the length of a feasibility interval is related to only parts of periods of tasks, e.g., LCM n-1 , then, a model's execution paradigm will play a role due to that some execution and preemption states must be considered, and thus a feasibility interval derived in one model may not be applicable to other models. Before introducing our method, the following results are needed. In [11], [13] and [14], the authors presented the periodicity of feasible schedule of periodic tasks, and we refer to a result in [13] as Theorem 3.1. Notice that a synchronous system can be seen as a special case of an asynchronous system with all release offsets being zero.

div.head: Theorem 3.1 ([13])
div.p: Any feasible schedule of an asynchronous system is finally periodic, i.e. periodic from some point.

Therefore, it may need to find the appropriate periodic point for determining feasibility interval of a given task set, and previous results on feasibility interval were derived from aiming at this goal. However, the length of schedulability testing interval has been neglected, which could be unbounded and very long. In the following we prove that the length of schedulability testing interval can in fact be bounded. Lemma 3.2. Consider a schedulable periodic n-task set * n = {τ 1 ,τ 2 ,...,τ n } under fixed priority scheduling, with arbitrary release offsets. Then, there must be some stabilization time point t z at which, for each task τ k , 1 d k d n, the relative time, r k ', between the point t z and the nearest release time of task τ k after that point is less than its period, i.e., t z d t z +r k '<t z +T k .

Proof. By Theorem 3.1, there is some periodic time point from which the schedule will repeat itself one after another. After that point, we randomly choose a time, denoted by t z , at which there is a release of some task, then, we prove that this time point t z satisfies the requirement. The idea is illustrated in Fig. 2.

For each task τ k , 1 d k d n, consider the relative time, r k ', between the point t z and the nearest release time of task τ k at or after that point t z . If r k '=0, it satisfies the requirement. If r k ' > 0, since this is the nearest release time after time t z , then, the time of the previous release of task τ k must be before the time t z . Clearly, the time elapsed between these two releases which are at different sides of time t z is the period of task τ k , i.e., T k , thus, there will be r k '<T k . Thus, the claim follows. □ Note that there are many such time points due to periodicity. div.p: It is known that the P-FRP model is of difference from the classical model in the execution paradigm. In the classical model, preempted jobs can resume execution from the point they were interrupted, however, in the P-FRP model, preempted jobs will roll back and restart execution anew from the very beginning, at some later time after higher priority jobs finish execution, i.e., non-finished lower priority jobs will be aborted. Therefore, the method proposed in [14] is only applicable to the classical model, not to the P-FRP model.

div.head: IV. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we identify limitations of previous results on schedulability testing intervals, and propose a transforming method for deriving a minimal schedulability testing interval for real-time periodic n-task sets with arbitrary release offsets under fixed priority scheduling on uniprocessor. The transformation complexity is O(n), and previous limitations are eliminated. Compared with previous results, the maximal length of a schedule constructed for checking the schedulability of * n is only LCM n in the classical model, and is bounded by min{) max +2•LCM n , S n +LCM n } in the P-FRP model in the worst case, where ) max is bounded by max 1 d j d n {T j -1} and S n by 6 1 d j d n (T j -1). We believe these results are helpful in both the theory and in practice engineering of schedulability analysis of real-time tasks under fixed priority preemptive scheduling. In the P-FRP model, the length of the schedulability testing interval might be shortened further and this is left for future work.
